input.question: Why do we define the point of no return from a black hole (Schwartzchild radius) with a speed, instead of total energy required?
input.ground_truth: In general relativity, the curvature of spacetime sort of flips when you cross the horizon. Space becomes timelike and time becomes spacelike. A consequence of this is that the only paths through spacetime are towards the center. Moving away from it is equivalent to going back in time. This is independent of the fact that the escape velocity on the surface is light speed.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why do we define the point of no return from a black hole (Schwartzchild radius) with a speed, instead of total energy required?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you’re on a playground slide. Once you go past a certain point, you can’t climb back up—you can only go down to the bottom. That special point on the slide is like the “point of no return” for a black hole. It’s called the **Schwarzschild radius**.

Now, imagine instead of saying “you can’t go back after this point,” someone said, “you need THIS MUCH energy to climb back up.” But that would be tricky, because how much energy you need depends on how heavy you are and how strong you are.

But the “point of no return” is simple: if you go past this invisible line around the black hole, you can’t escape, no matter how strong or energetic you are. That’s why scientists use a **speed** (called the “escape velocity”) to define this point. It’s like saying, “If you’re going faster than THIS, you can’t come back.” It’s an easy way to tell everyone where the danger zone starts, just by looking at how fast something is moving.

So, it’s easier to say, “Go past this line and you can’t get out!” instead of trying to explain how much energy everyone needs, because that would be different for every person (or every bit of stuff).
